title: Rethinking Epistemic Uncertainty in Node Classification through Information Growth

paper.title: Rethinking Epistemic Uncertainty in Node Classification through Information Growth
paper.abstract: Abstract Epistemic uncertainty should decrease as additional information about the data-generating process (DGP) becomes available to the predictor. Yet, existing graph evidential deep learning (EDL) methods for node classification typically construct epistemic uncertainty from graph-specific properties and evaluate it on downstream tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not test its reducibility as information about the DGP increases. To make reducibility directly testable, we introduce a statistical framework for studying epistemic uncertainty under information growth. Our framework specifies an information-growth experimental protocol and a consistency criterion for epistemic predictors, while using projective graph DGPs to ensure that growing graphs, which in general need not provide increasing information about the same DGP, constitute coherent observations of the same underlying process. We show that EDL methods do not explicitly estimate data uncertainty arising from a single finite graph observation and instead regulate epistemic uncertainty through model hyperparameters, precluding consistency, as corroborated by controlled information-growth experiments. As an alternative, we propose graph bootstrap ensembles, capturing both data and procedural uncertainty through graph resampling and randomized training. Under the same experimental protocol, these ensembles exhibit epistemic uncertainty reduction beyond standard deep ensembles. These findings support bootstrap ensembles as candidate consistent epistemic predictors under information growth.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Machine learning models are increasingly expected to provide not only accurate predictions, but also reliable estimates of predictive uncertainty ( Abdar et al., 2021 ; Gawlikowski et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Predictive uncertainty is commonly decomposed into aleatoric uncertainty, arising from intrinsic ambiguity in the data-generating process (DGP) and thus irreducible, and epistemic uncertainty, arising from limited knowledge of that process and thus reducible with additional data ( Hüllermeier and Waegeman, 2021 ; Sale et al., 2026 ) . In classical supervised learning with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, under suitable regularity conditions, epistemic uncertainty is operationally characterized to decrease monotonically as information increases and eventually vanish ( Bengs et al., 2022 ; Juergens et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) . Extending this characterization to node classification on graphs is non-trivial. While increasing sample size provides a natural information-growth mechanism in the i.i.d. setting, no analogous mechanism is readily available for node classification. Intuitively, information growth would involve progressively larger graph observations and training sets becoming available, allowing predictors to be retrained on more informative observations for the same node classification problem. However, nodes are dependent, and observing more of them does not necessarily yield more information about the same underlying DGP ( Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013 ) . Consequently, node classification currently lacks a framework for assessing the reducibility of epistemic uncertainty under information growth. Graph uncertainty quantification has been studied using a variety of approaches (see Wang et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2024) for reviews). Among these, evidential deep learning (EDL) methods ( Zhao et al., 2020 ; Stadler et al., 2021 ; Hart et al., 2023 ; Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024b ; Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024a ) are particularly relevant because they make the epistemic interpretation a central modeling objective, prescribing appropriate uncertainty behavior through graph-specific principles, including reducibility through feature support and structural support , and the reducibility or irreducibility due to neighborhood conflict . However, these principles are defined with respect to the features and topology of a fixed observed graph rather than under information growth. Empirical evaluations likewise assess epistemic uncertainty through its utility for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, whose optimal predictors need not coincide with predictors of reducible epistemic uncertainty ( Paplhám et al., 2026 ) . While informative about task-specific downstream utility, such evaluations therefore cannot establish whether an uncertainty score has this epistemic interpretation. Together, these limitations raise fundamental questions about how epistemic uncertainty should be defined and modeled in node classification. We investigate these issues through three research questions: (RQ1) What constitutes a principled statistical framework for epistemic predictors in node classification? (RQ2) Are graph EDL models consistent epistemic predictors, and, if not, what are their fundamental limitations? (RQ3) Which alternative approach can address these limitations? Contributions. We address these questions through three main contributions. (1) We establish the first statistical framework for epistemic uncertainty under information growth in node classification, comprising an information-growth experimental protocol and a definition of consistent epistemic predictors. The former naturally requires projective graph DGPs to preserve the underlying node-classification problem across nested graphs and learning tasks ( Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013 ) , while the latter requires decreasing and asymptotically vanishing uncertainty. Together, these provide a statistical basis for assessing epistemic reducibility beyond conventional evaluations. (2) We unify graph EDL objectives and characterize their population optima, showing how model hyperparameters artificially regulate epistemic uncertainty in the absence of explicit estimation of data uncertainty ( Shen et al., 2024 ) , arising from observing a single finite realization of the DGP, ultimately precluding epistemic consistency. Controlled information-growth experiments on projective graphs confirm insufficient epistemic concentration and persistent parameterization dependence, corroborating the structural limitations that undermine their use as consistent epistemic predictors. (3) Motivated by evidence that bootstrap-based ensembles capture data and procedural uncertainty ( Jimenez et al., 2026 ) , thus enabling decreasing epistemic uncertainty in the i.i.d. setting ( Jain and Bates, 2025 ) , we extend this approach to graphs through graph bootstrap ensembles . Under the same protocol as in (2), the experiments support these ensembles as a family of candidate consistent epistemic predictors, demonstrating the ability to recover epistemic concentration absent from standard deep ensembles. Together, these contributions establish a statistical foundation for understanding epistemic uncertainty in node classification, reveal the limitations of existing evidential approaches when assessed through information growth, and introduce graph bootstrap ensembles as a theoretically motivated, empirically supported alternative for modeling epistemic uncertainty that contracts under information growth.

sections.heading: 2.2 Why Evaluate Epistemic Uncertainty under Information Growth?
sections.text: Epistemic uncertainty is commonly considered useful a priori for downstream tasks such as OOD detection on graphs, as the lack of model knowledge about OOD inputs is expected to result in higher epistemic uncertainty ( Bazhenov et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , and performance on these benchmarks is therefore used to assess the quality of EDL uncertainty estimates. However, our results show that the most effective uncertainty type depends on the particular model and OOD protocol, with AU/TU typically performing best for leave-out-classes (LOC) and feature isolation (FI) with Bernoulli perturbations, and EU for Gaussian FI (Table 1 ; additional results in Appendix F ). That non-epistemic components can outperform EU supports growing criticism that OOD discrimination and the reducibility of epistemic uncertainty under increasing information constitute distinct objectives whose optimal predictors need not coincide ( Li et al., 2025 ; Paplhám et al., 2026 ) . sections.heading: 3 A Statistical Framework for Graph Epistemic Uncertainty
sections.text: Addressing (RQ1) , we extend the i.i.d. characterization of epistemic predictors ( Bengs et al., 2022 ; Juergens et al., 2024 ) to node classification by defining a statistical framework with an information-growth experimental protocol and a consistency criterion for epistemic predictors.

sections.heading: 3.1 Information-Growth Experimental Protocol
sections.text: Constructing an information-growth experimental protocol for node classification requires three components: (i) the sampling unit , i.e., what constitutes one observation from the DGP; (ii) the sampling scheme , i.e., how increasingly informative observations are generated from the same DGP; and (iii) the learning task , i.e., how the supervised prediction problem evolves along this sequence. Sampling unit. Unlike classical datasets, the nodes of a graph are not a collection of i.i.d. observations. We therefore take the observed graph 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ ) {\mathcal{G}}=({\mathcal{V}},{\mathcal{E}}) , equivalently the subgraph induced by 𝒱 {\mathcal{V}} , as the sampling unit, following the graph-as-observation perspective of Shalizi and Rinaldo (2013) . Increasing information then corresponds to observing nested graphs 𝒢 ⊂ 𝒢 ′ {\mathcal{G}}\subset{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime} , with 𝒱 ⊂ 𝒱 ′ {\mathcal{V}}\subset{\mathcal{V}}^{\prime} and 𝒢 {\mathcal{G}} equal to the subgraph of 𝒢 ′ {\mathcal{G}}^{\prime} induced by 𝒱 {\mathcal{V}} . Sampling scheme. Requiring two nested graphs to arise from the same DGP is non-trivial. This consistency is implicit in the i.i.d. setting, where every finite sample is a restriction of the same infinite sequence, but need not hold across graphs of different sizes. We make it explicit through projectibility ( Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013 ) . Let 𝒜 {\mathcal{A}} be a collection of finite subsets of a countable node index set 𝕀 \mathbb{I} , ordered by inclusion, and let { ℙ A , ϕ } A ∈ 𝒜 , ϕ ∈ Φ \{\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi}\}_{A\in{\mathcal{A}},\phi\in\Phi} denote a family of finite-dimensional DGPs, where G A ∼ ℙ A , ϕ G_{A}\sim\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi} denotes the attributed graph indexed by A A . For A ⊂ B A\subset B , let π B → A \pi_{B\to A} denote the natural projection that restricts an observation indexed by B B to the indices in A A . Definition 3.1 (Projective DGP) . The family { ℙ A , ϕ } A ∈ 𝒜 , ϕ ∈ Φ \{\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi}\}_{A\in{\mathcal{A}},\phi\in\Phi} is projective if, for every A ⊂ B A\subset B , ℙ A , ϕ = ℙ B , ϕ ∘ π B → A − 1 ∀ ϕ ∈ Φ . \mathbb{P}_{A,\phi}=\mathbb{P}_{B,\phi}\circ\pi^{-1}_{B\to A}\qquad\forall\phi\in\Phi. (7) Thus, projectibility gives a coherent meaning to information growth by ensuring that every smaller observation has exactly the distribution obtained by marginalizing any larger observation under the stochastic process with the same parameter ϕ \phi . Moreover, by the Kolmogorov extension theorem ( Kallenberg, 1997 ) , every such projective family uniquely defines an infinite-dimensional distribution ℙ ϕ \mathbb{P}_{\phi} whose finite-dimensional marginals are precisely { ℙ A , ϕ } A ∈ 𝒜 \{\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi}\}_{A\in{\mathcal{A}}} . Dense graphons are an important class of projective graph families ( Veitch and Roy, 2015 ) and will serve as the concrete instantiation of this framework in our experiments. Other prominent graph models, including many exponential random graph models and sparse random graph formulations, are not projective ( Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013 ; Schweinberger et al., 2017 ) . Learning task. Finally, the supervised tasks induced by increasingly large graph observations must exploit the corresponding information growth. If 𝒯 ( tr ) ⊂ 𝒱 {\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}\subset{\mathcal{V}} and 𝒯 ′ ( tr ) ⊂ 𝒱 ′ {\mathcal{T}}^{\prime(\mathrm{tr})}\subset{\mathcal{V}}^{\prime} denote the training sets associated with 𝒢 ⊂ 𝒢 ′ {\mathcal{G}}\subset{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime} , respectively, we require 𝒯 ( tr ) ⊂ 𝒯 ′ ( tr ) {\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}\subset{\mathcal{T}}^{\prime(\mathrm{tr})} , so that each larger task extends the previous one with additional information about the same underlying node-classification problem. Validation and test sets are defined analogously.

sections.heading: 5 Graph Bootstrap Ensembles
sections.text: The previous analysis motivates constructing a second-order predictor whose uncertainty is tied explicitly to the information available about the graph DGP. We pursue this idea through graph bootstrap ensembles (GB-Ens), extending deep ensembles, an already understudied approach in node classification ( Vieira et al., 2026 ) , to the largely unexplored setting of graph bootstrapping. For each of B B bootstrap graph realizations, we train S S independently initialized GNNs, mirroring i.i.d. bootstrap ensembles that combine procedural and data variability through resampling ( Juergens et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2024 ; Jain and Bates, 2025 ; Jimenez et al., 2026 ) . The ability to represent both recognized sources of epistemic uncertainty ( Jain and Bates, 2025 ; Jimenez et al., 2026 ) provides a key motivation for using bootstrap ensembles rather than alternative second-order predictors, including EDL models and deep ensembles, which may fail to capture one or both sources. In the i.i.d. setting, bootstrap-based MI has also been shown, under suitable conditions, to converge asymptotically to its Bayesian counterpart ( Jain and Bates, 2025 ) , providing theoretical support for bootstrap-based epistemic uncertainty estimation with neural networks. For graphs, however, bootstrap guarantees remain restricted to specific combinations of graph DGPs, bootstrap schemes, and estimation targets ( Schmid and Desmarais, 2017 ; Levin and Levina, 2019 ; Green and Shalizi, 2022 ; Lin et al., 2020 ; Shao and Le, 2024 ) , with no analogous result for MI. Nevertheless, projective synthetic graph DGPs whose sampling process can be accurately approximated by a bootstrap procedure provide a tractable setting for studying whether graph bootstrap ensembles empirically exhibit the consistent information-growth behavior of Definition 3.2 , analogous to that established in the i.i.d. setting. GB-Ens is also computationally feasible despite increased total cost, through parallel training and sequential inference; see Appendix G for computational comparisons. Uncertainty decomposition. sections.text: We empirically address (RQ2) – (RQ3) through controlled experiments on synthetic projective graph DGPs. For (RQ2) , we validate our analysis of graph EDL uncertainty under information growth. For (RQ3) , we assess graph bootstrap ensembles as an alternative approach to epistemic prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/emmamenegh/Research-Code-Release . Models. We evaluate S-BGCN-K and S-BGCN-T-K ( Zhao et al., 2020 ) , GPN ( Stadler et al., 2021 ) , GPN-GD EVI and GPN-GD LAT ( Hart et al., 2023 ) , GPN-LOP ( Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024b ) , CUQ-APPNP, CUQ-GAT, and CUQ-GCN ( Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024a ) as EDL baselines, and GB-Ens with APPNP, GAT, and GCN architectures. Each GB-Ens comprises 25 × 4 25\times 4 models, corresponding to 25 25 bootstrap samples and 4 4 random seeds per sample. Model parameterizations are reported in Appendix D . Datasets. Our experiments comprise two synthetic projective graphon DGPs. The synthetic DGPs are an exponential-decay graphon and an assortative stochastic-block model (SBM), which define complementary continuous- and discrete-structure regimes for a balanced seven-class node-classification problem. For each DGP, we generate 20 20 independent replicates of a projective sequence, with six graph sizes logarithmically spaced between 500 500 and 10,000 10{,}000 nodes. At each graph size, we use 5 % / 15 % / 80 % 5\%/15\%/80\% class-stratified train/validation/test splits constructed according to the protocol in Section 3.1 and fixed across bootstrap replicates for each observed graph. Full DGP specifications and graphon statistics are reported in Appendices B and C . RQ2: Graph EDL models are inconsistent epistemic predictors. We examine whether the uncertainty behavior of graph EDL models characterized at the nonparametric population optimum by Theorem 4.3 persists with finite data and parametric models. We assess both EU concentration with increasing information and the dependence of EU and AU on model parameterization. At N = 10,000 N=10{,}000 , varying the EDL regularization parameter λ \lambda reveals substantial changes in AU on the same observed graph (Figure 1(b) ), demonstrating its dependence on model parameterization rather than on the DGP alone. Figure 2(a) shows mean GB-Ens epistemic uncertainty across 20 20 projective-sequence replicates of the exponential-decay graphon, with pointwise 95 % 95\% bootstrap CIs. From N = 500 N=500 to N = 10,000 N=10{,}000 , EU decreases monotonically by 94 % 94\% for GCN, 91 % 91\% for APPNP, and 61 % 61\% for GAT. On the SBM (Appendix E ), EU similarly decreases substantially for APPNP and GCN, whereas GAT shows a weaker, non-monotonic reduction due to persistent randomized-training variability, plausibly reflecting its sensitivity to learned attention weights and additional attention dropout. The decomposition in Figure 2(b) further shows comparable randomized-seed and bootstrap contributions to EU that decrease with increasing information, with relative magnitude depending on the backbone and DGP. Finally, Figure 3(b) shows that GB-Ens AU decreases and eventually stabilizes, with all three backbones approaching similar plateaus, consistent with convergence toward a predictor-independent estimate of aleatoric uncertainty. The same behavior is observed for the SBM (Appendix E ). To assess the effect of graph resampling, we compare GB-Ens with standard graph deep ensembles (G-Ens), trained with 10 10 different random seeds on the observed graph using the same backbones. Figure 3(a) shows that, on the exponential-decay graphon, G-Ens exhibit no consistent EU contraction, while Figure 3(b) shows strongly backbone-dependent AU trajectories, with GAT trending upward and GCN continuing to decrease. Similar behavior is observed on the SBM (Appendix E ). Moreover, the gap between G-Ens EU and the randomized-training component of GB-Ens widens with graph size, as the latter contracts under information growth while the former does not. Graph resampling therefore does not simply add bootstrap variability, but induces convergent behavior also in the seed component, enabling EU contraction that is not observed for standard deep ensembles. As a simple diagnostic of GB-Ens’s approximation to the full second-order distribution induced by true-DGP resampling, which captures predictive variability without DGP estimation error, we compare the two distributions using normalized node-wise Wasserstein-1 distances. Similar results on the SBM are reported in Appendix E , suggesting that approximation quality varies across predictors. sections.heading: 7 Conclusions
sections.text: Take-home message. Epistemic uncertainty in node classification should be assessed through its behavior under increasing information, rather than solely by obeying principles or being useful for downstream tasks on a fixed graph. This perspective identifies consistent epistemic uncertainty as requiring estimates that reflect data uncertainty rather than remaining hyperparameter-dependent, a requirement generally not met by graph EDL models. GB-Ens provides a constructive approach by capturing data and procedural uncertainty, with controlled experiments supporting it as a family of candidate consistent predictors. Limitations & future work. The theoretical consistency of bootstrap-based graph epistemic predictors remains to be established. Moreover, information-growth behavior cannot be evaluated on standard real-world benchmarks, which lack the sampling process required to generate increasingly informative observations from the same DGP. Benchmarks leveraging real graph-growth mechanisms, where projectibility is often natural ( Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013 ) , could extend our analysis beyond synthetic random graphs, either retaining node classification and motivating improved bootstrap-based predictors or considering tasks more naturally aligned with graph growth.

sections.text: We consider two complementary homophilic graph DGPs: a smooth exponential-decay graphon, representing continuous latent similarity, and an assortative stochastic block model (SBM) graphon, representing discrete community structure, both commonly considered in the literature ( Xu et al., 2021 ) . Besides providing qualitatively different graph structure, the SBM connects our construction to projective dyadic-independence models studied within the exponential random-graph model framework of Shalizi and Rinaldo (2013) . Both follow the graphon construction U i \displaystyle U_{i} ∼ iid ​ Unif ​ ( 0 , 1 ) , \displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathrm{Unif}(0,1), (37) A i ​ j | U i , U j \displaystyle A_{ij}|U_{i},U_{j} ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( W ⁡ ( U i , U j ) ) , \displaystyle\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(W(U_{i},U_{j})), (38) where W : [ 0 , 1 ] 2 → [ 0 , 1 ] W:[0,1]^{2}\rightarrow[0,1] maps pairs of latent positions to edge probabilities. For the exponential-decay graphon, this mapping depends directly on the distance between latent positions, W exp ​ ( U i , U j ) = exp ⁡ ( − β ​ | U i − U j | ) , W_{\mathrm{exp}}(U_{i},U_{j})=\exp(-\beta|U_{i}-U_{j}|), (39) such that connectivity decreases smoothly with latent distance. For the SBM graphon, the latent space is instead partitioned into K K blocks through a mapping b : [ 0 , 1 ] → { 1 , … , K } b:[0,1]\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,K\} . Edge probabilities are then determined by the corresponding entries of an assortative block probability matrix P P , yielding the step-function graphon W SBM ​ ( U i , U j ) = P b ⁡ ( U i ) , b ⁡ ( U j ) . (42) For the exponential-decay graphon, class probabilities vary smoothly over the latent space, with greater label ambiguity near transitions between neighboring classes. For the SBM graphon, class probabilities follow the block structure but vary smoothly within blocks, with greater ambiguity near block transitions. Each node additionally receives 12 noisy continuous and binary features that are informative of the latent class structure without deterministically identifying the observed label. Feature informativeness is likewise allowed to vary with latent position, such that graph structure and node features provide complementary and imperfect information about the class. sections.heading: Appendix G Computational Complexity
sections.text: Graph EDL methods can themselves incur substantial computational costs, with different methods trading off preprocessing, training, inference, and memory requirements. Ensemble-based methods require repeated model fitting, but retain manageable per-model computation and peak memory and are naturally parallelizable. GPN and CUQ-GCN admit O ⁡ ( N + M ) O(N+M) implementations, whereas GPN-LOP and S-BGCN-K can incur O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) computation due to dense propagation and pairwise GKDE prior construction, respectively. For GCN-based ensembles, training costs O ⁡ ( N + M ) O(N+M) per member; GB-Ens additionally requires bootstrap generation, whose cost depends on the k k -NN construction and can reach O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) for general similarity search, although cheaper alternatives are available, such as the open Jaccard similarity metric used in our experiments. Bootstrap generation is repeated for each bootstrap sample. Across ensemble members, training cost scales linearly for both GB-Ens and G-Ens but is naturally parallelizable. Moreover, processing members independently and accumulating uncertainty statistics online keeps peak memory at O ⁡ ( N + M ) O(N+M) , comparable to GPN, CUQ-GNN, and S-BGCN-K, whereas GPN-LOP can require O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) memory due to dense propagation. Tables 21 , 22 and 23 complement the asymptotic analysis with empirical measurements on CoraML, CoauthorPhysics and OGBN-ArXiv, obtained on a dedicated NVIDIA A100 64 GB GPU. GB-Ens uses 100 models in the 25 × 4 25\times 4 bootstrap–seed decomposition, while G-Ens uses 10 randomly initialized models. Preprocessing time reports the total preprocessing cost required by each method, including generation of all bootstrap samples for GB-Ens. Epoch time is reported per model and training epoch, while inference time reports the total cost of producing one uncertainty estimate, aggregating the 100 forward passes required by GB-Ens and S-BGCN variants and the 10 forward passes required by G-Ens. Peak inference memory is measured when processing ensemble members sequentially. GB-Ens therefore trades increased total preprocessing, training, and inference costs for moderate peak memory requirements: graph bootstrapping becomes particularly costly on larger graphs, while its 100 members can be trained independently and in parallel, and sequential inference limits peak memory. This trade-off differs across EDL baselines: some avoid repeated model fitting and inference, whereas preprocessing-heavy methods such as S-BGCN-K incur comparable preprocessing costs on OGBN-ArXiv, and dense propagation makes GPN-LOP considerably more expensive on CoauthorPhysics and infeasible on OGBN-ArXiv under the available GPU memory. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.03418v1 [cs.LG] 02 Oct 2026 Rethinking Epistemic Uncertainty in Node Classification through Information Growth Emma Meneghini Affiliation: University of Trento Affiliation: Fondazione Bruno Kessler, FBK Francesco Ferrini Affiliation: Fondazione Bruno Kessler, FBK Bruno Lepri Affiliation: Fondazione Bruno Kessler, FBK Andrea Passerini Affiliation: University of Trento Veronica Lachi Affiliation: University of Tromsø Abstract Epistemic uncertainty should decrease as additional information about the data-generating process (DGP) becomes available to the predictor. Yet, existing graph evidential deep learning (EDL) methods for node classification typically construct epistemic uncertainty from graph-specific properties and evaluate it on downstream tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not test its reducibility as information about the DGP increases. To make reducibility directly testable, we introduce a statistical framework for studying epistemic uncertainty under information growth. Our framework specifies an information-growth experimental protocol and a consistency criterion for epistemic predictors, while using projective graph DGPs to ensure that growing graphs, which in general need not provide increasing information about the same DGP, constitute coherent observations of the same underlying process. We show that EDL methods do not explicitly estimate data uncertainty arising from a single finite graph observation and instead regulate epistemic uncertainty through model hyperparameters, precluding consistency, as corroborated by controlled information-growth experiments. As an alternative, we propose graph bootstrap ensembles, capturing both data and procedural uncertainty through graph resampling and randomized training. Under the same experimental protocol, these ensembles exhibit epistemic uncertainty reduction beyond standard deep ensembles. These findings support bootstrap ensembles as candidate consistent epistemic predictors under information growth. 1 Introduction Machine learning models are increasingly expected to provide not only accurate predictions, but also reliable estimates of predictive uncertainty ( Abdar et al., 2021 ; Gawlikowski et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Predictive uncertainty is commonly decomposed into aleatoric uncertainty, arising from intrinsic ambiguity in the data-generating process (DGP) and thus irreducible, and epistemic uncertainty, arising from limited knowledge of that process and thus reducible with additional data ( Hüllermeier and Waegeman, 2021 ; Sale et al., 2026 ) . In classical supervised learning with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, under suitable regularity conditions, epistemic uncertainty is operationally characterized to decrease monotonically as information increases and eventually vanish ( Bengs et al., 2022 ; Juergens et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) . Extending this characterization to node classification on graphs is non-trivial. While increasing sample size provides a natural information-growth mechanism in the i.i.d. setting, no analogous mechanism is readily available for node classification. Intuitively, information growth would involve progressively larger graph observations and training sets becoming available, allowing predictors to be retrained on more informative observations for the same node classification problem. However, nodes are dependent, and observing more of them does not necessarily yield more information about the same underlying DGP ( Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013 ) . Consequently, node classification currently lacks a framework for assessing the reducibility of epistemic uncertainty under information growth. Graph uncertainty quantification has been studied using a variety of approaches (see Wang et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2024) for reviews). Among these, evidential deep learning (EDL) methods ( Zhao et al., 2020 ; Stadler et al., 2021 ; Hart et al., 2023 ; Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024b ; Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024a ) are particularly relevant because they make the epistemic interpretation a central modeling objective, prescribing appropriate uncertainty behavior through graph-specific principles, including reducibility through feature support and structural support , and the reducibility or irreducibility due to neighborhood conflict . However, these principles are defined with respect to the features and topology of a fixed observed graph rather than under information growth. Empirical evaluations likewise assess epistemic uncertainty through its utility for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, whose optimal predictors need not coincide with predictors of reducible epistemic uncertainty ( Paplhám et al., 2026 ) . While informative about task-specific downstream utility, such evaluations therefore cannot establish whether an uncertainty score has this epistemic interpretation. Together, these limitations raise fundamental questions about how epistemic uncertainty should be defined and modeled in node classification. We investigate these issues through three research questions: (RQ1) What constitutes a principled statistical framework for epistemic predictors in node classification? (RQ2) Are graph EDL models consistent epistemic predictors, and, if not, what are their fundamental limitations? (RQ3) Which alternative approach can address these limitations? Contributions. We address these questions through three main contributions. (1) We establish the first statistical framework for epistemic uncertainty under information growth in node classification, comprising an information-growth experimental protocol and a definition of consistent epistemic predictors. The former naturally requires projective graph DGPs to preserve the underlying node-classification problem across nested graphs and learning tasks ( Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013 ) , while the latter requires decreasing and asymptotically vanishing uncertainty. Together, these provide a statistical basis for assessing epistemic reducibility beyond conventional evaluations. (2) We unify graph EDL objectives and characterize their population optima, showing how model hyperparameters artificially regulate epistemic uncertainty in the absence of explicit estimation of data uncertainty ( Shen et al., 2024 ) , arising from observing a single finite realization of the DGP, ultimately precluding epistemic consistency. Controlled information-growth experiments on projective graphs confirm insufficient epistemic concentration and persistent parameterization dependence, corroborating the structural limitations that undermine their use as consistent epistemic predictors. (3) Motivated by evidence that bootstrap-based ensembles capture data and procedural uncertainty ( Jimenez et al., 2026 ) , thus enabling decreasing epistemic uncertainty in the i.i.d. setting ( Jain and Bates, 2025 ) , we extend this approach to graphs through graph bootstrap ensembles . Under the same protocol as in (2), the experiments support these ensembles as a family of candidate consistent epistemic predictors, demonstrating the ability to recover epistemic concentration absent from standard deep ensembles. Together, these contributions establish a statistical foundation for understanding epistemic uncertainty in node classification, reveal the limitations of existing evidential approaches when assessed through information growth, and introduce graph bootstrap ensembles as a theoretically motivated, empirically supported alternative for modeling epistemic uncertainty that contracts under information growth. 2 Background on Predictive Uncertainty and Motivation Let 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ ) {\mathcal{G}}=({\mathcal{V}},{\mathcal{E}}) be an undirected attributed graph with | 𝒱 | = N |{\mathcal{V}}|=N , adjacency matrix A ∈ { 0 , 1 } N × N A\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N} , and node feature matrix X ∈ ℝ N × D X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} . Sampling unit. Unlike classical datasets, the nodes of a graph are not a collection of i.i.d. observations. We therefore take the observed graph 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ ) {\mathcal{G}}=({\mathcal{V}},{\mathcal{E}}) , equivalently the subgraph induced by 𝒱 {\mathcal{V}} , as the sampling unit, following the graph-as-observation perspective of Shalizi and Rinaldo (2013) . Increasing information then corresponds to observing nested graphs 𝒢 ⊂ 𝒢 ′ {\mathcal{G}}\subset{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime} , with 𝒱 ⊂ 𝒱 ′ {\mathcal{V}}\subset{\mathcal{V}}^{\prime} and 𝒢 {\mathcal{G}} equal to the subgraph of 𝒢 ′ {\mathcal{G}}^{\prime} induced by 𝒱 {\mathcal{V}} . This consistency is implicit in the i.i.d. setting, where every finite sample is a restriction of the same infinite sequence, but need not hold across graphs of different sizes. We pursue this idea through graph bootstrap ensembles (GB-Ens), extending deep ensembles, an already understudied approach in node classification ( Vieira et al., 2026 ) , to the largely unexplored setting of graph bootstrapping. For each of B B bootstrap graph realizations, we train S S independently initialized GNNs, mirroring i.i.d. bootstrap ensembles that combine procedural and data variability through resampling ( Juergens et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2024 ; Jain and Bates, 2025 ; Jimenez et al., 2026 ) . The ability to represent both recognized sources of epistemic uncertainty ( Jain and Bates, 2025 ; Jimenez et al., 2026 ) provides a key motivation for using bootstrap ensembles rather than alternative second-order predictors, including EDL models and deep ensembles, which may fail to capture one or both sources. In the i.i.d. setting, bootstrap-based MI has also been shown, under suitable conditions, to converge asymptotically to its Bayesian counterpart ( Jain and Bates, 2025 ) , providing theoretical support for bootstrap-based epistemic uncertainty estimation with neural networks. For graphs, however, bootstrap guarantees remain restricted to specific combinations of graph DGPs, bootstrap schemes, and estimation targets ( Schmid and Desmarais, 2017 ; Levin and Levina, 2019 ; Green and Shalizi, 2022 ; Lin et al., 2020 ; Shao and Le, 2024 ) , with no analogous result for MI. Nevertheless, projective synthetic graph DGPs whose sampling process can be accurately approximated by a bootstrap procedure provide a tractable setting for studying whether graph bootstrap ensembles empirically exhibit the consistent information-growth behavior of Definition 3.2 , analogous to that established in the i.i.d. setting. Graph resampling. To instantiate the graph-resampling component of GB-Ens, we adopt a local non-parametric bootstrap adapted from Jeong and Donnat (2025) , developed under an exchangeable graphon model. It estimates asymptotically unbiased edge probabilities from the observed connectivity of similar nodes and samples graph realizations accordingly. We use an edge-only bootstrap that retains node identities, features, and labels across realizations, thereby preserving the node classification task while capturing sampling variability in the graph structure.
